book: 010 - Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy

chapters.file: ch23 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Jorge Gracia reframes the fidelity controversy as a problem in the theory of interpretation: Gibson had to make countless choices the Gospels leave silent (Christ's worn clothing, the Italian landscape, Jesus staring into the camera at the Last Supper, added scenes like Satan raging and demon children haunting Judas), so the film is unavoidably an interpretation. He surveys five criteria interpreters of Scripture have used — personal intuition (illustrated by Augustine's 'take and read' in the Confessions), ecclesial authority and the visions of nuns Emmerich and Agreda, sola scriptura, historical scholarship, and tradition (Aquinas's camp; Veronica's veil, the Shroud, the virgin Mary's prominence) — and argues each is inadequate alone because every one rests on prior theology. Hence disputes about the film are really disputes between theologies, and the film makes sense only within Gibson's Catholic view of Jesus as the Messiah announced by Isaiah 53.

chapters.file: ch24 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Cynthia Freeland reads the film's women through feminist ethics of care: the two Marys function like a Greek-chorus of grieving observers, while Claudia and Veronica — and the casting of Bellucci as the repentant whore opposite Morgenstern's ageless Madonna — lock them into the virgin/whore double bind. Using Carol Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg's Kantian standard and Nel Noddings's and Sara Ruddick's point that mothering is reflective 'attentive' work, she argues Gibson's Mary is one-dimensional: flashbacks of 'I am here' show maternal instinct, never moral deliberation. She ends by suggesting the historical Jesus, like Socrates, was more radical toward women than the film, and that Irigaray's reading of Christ's bleeding wounds as a feminized maternal body sits oddly with Gibson's muscular, 'take it like a man' Savior.

chapters.file: ch25 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
ch26 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.

chapters.file: ch27 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Gareth Matthews contrasts Plato's serene Phaedo — Socrates conducting a seminar on immortality, death as the cure for life's ills, 'we owe a cock to Asclepius' — with Gibson's prolonged torture, while noting deep parallels: both men were condemned by large courts on religious charges (impiety, blasphemy) with political subtexts. Socrates in the Apology models facing death through Socratic ignorance ('to fear death is to think oneself wise when one is not'), and Matthews argues Gibson's magnified suffering makes Christ an icon of an atonement nobody could imitate rather than a model for our own deaths; only the Gethsemane prayer and 'why hast thou forsaken me' (read via Cullmann) can actually help a believer face dying.

chapters.file: ch28 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bruce Reichenbach reads the film's choreographed pas de deux as three distinct theories of atonement: the conquest dance with Satan in Gethsemane (crushing the serpent of Genesis 3:15, Satan's final scream) enacts the Christus victor view of the Church Fathers; Simon of Cyrene's reluctant co-bearing of the cross illustrates Abelard's moral-influence view, though Gibson shows resilient fortitude rather than the love Abelard's theory requires to transform Simon; and Mary's mirrored 'parallel dance' makes her a co-redemptrix sharing her son's agony. Against this he sets Heidegger — Jesus grasps his death with anticipatory resolve, thrownness, and the 'moment of vision' with Mary, but dies for the Other rather than to authenticate his own life — and faults the film for omitting Anselm's (and Swinburne's) substitutionary atonement entirely: no sin, repentance, reparation, or penance appears, unlike Maximilian Kolbe's real substitution at Auschwitz.

chapters.file: ch29 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Paul Moser answers the objection that an all-loving God could not plan His Son's torture by arguing the cross is God's scandalous self-giving love: Jesus is no mere moral guru but the unique atoning sacrifice (the mad/Satanic/Son-of-God trilemma, 'he who delivered me to you has the greater sin'), and the crucifixion is God's grand reversal where self-giving love defeats death. He attacks the 'nice god' of natural theology as domesticating idolatry — God hides His plans from 'the wise and the intelligent' — and holds that we know God not by philosophical evidence but through Gethsemane-style filial obedience ('not my will but yours'), noting that Gibson himself appears in the film driving a nail, casting all of us as the crucifiers whom God forgives.

chapters.file: ch30 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
ch31 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Jonathan Sanford distinguishes necessity of the end, of compulsion, and of nature to argue Christ's passion was both necessary and free: justice requires reparation for the harmony Adam and Eve broke, God cannot simply waive it without making a mockery of sin, yet no compulsion operates on Christ — unlike the blind inner drives Nietzsche's will to power or Schopenhauer's will would represent. Using Aristotle, he argues Christ's fully virtuous character (practical wisdom plus courage and temperance become a 'second nature') makes disobedience nearly unimaginable, and his divinity makes it impossible, so his choice 'could not have been different' precisely because it was perfectly free; the Gethsemane agony shows not division in the God-man but the difficulty of holding his human and divine wills in unity.

chapters.file: ch32 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.

chapters.file: ch33 - Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.

holes.name: Hermeneutics (interpretation of revelation)
holes.what: The theory of how texts — especially texts regarded as divine revelation — should be interpreted, weighing personal intuition, authority, the text itself, historical scholarship, and tradition.
holes.why: Chapter 23's entire argument is that judging the film's fidelity to the Gospels requires a hermeneutics of Scripture on top of faith, and taxonomy has no concept for interpretation theory.

holes.name: Divine Hiddenness (deus absconditus)
holes.what: The idea that God deliberately hides — Isaiah's 'God who hides himself' — so that people can freely choose or reject him rather than be coerced by overwhelming evidence of his presence.
holes.why: Chapter 26 builds its whole account of Christ's strategy and faith on the hidden God, and chapter 29 likewise treats God's elusiveness as the condition of genuinely knowing him.

holes.name: Theories of Atonement (Christus Victor, Satisfaction, Moral Influence)
holes.what: Competing Christian accounts of how Christ's suffering and death reconciles humanity to God: conquest of the demonic (Christus victor), payment of the debt we owe God (Anselm's satisfaction), or a transforming moral example (Abelard).
holes.why: Chapter 28's entire reading of the film maps each pas de deux onto a different atonement theory, which no taxonomy concept covers.

holes.name: Christian Pacifism / Nonresistance
holes.what: The doctrine, drawn from Jesus's 'resist not evil' and 'turn the other cheek,' that followers should renounce violence and not resist evil, even at the cost of suffering.
holes.why: Chapter 33 is devoted to interpreting and defending Jesus's nonviolence, and taxonomy lacks any pacifism or nonviolence concept (ahimsa is Gandhi's distinct Hindu-derived doctrine).
